title: God is charity (1 John 4:8)
hookLine: the Douay calls it charity: God's very being is love (CCC 221)

cards: Say the word charity today and people picture a donation: a jar by the register, a fundraiser, a tax receipt in January. Good things, but a little distant.
So it's a jolt to open an old Catholic Bible, the Douay-Rheims, and find this plainly in the first letter of John: God is charity. Not God gives to charity. God is charity.
That old English word once meant something much bigger and warmer than a donation. Today: agape.

teach.b: First, the verse. In the Douay-Rheims: "He that loveth not, knoweth not God: for God is charity." And a few lines later: "God is charity: and he that abideth in charity, abideth in God, and God in him."

The Greek word is agape, the love that gives itself away for another's good. Saint Jerome's Latin Bible put it as Deus caritas est, and the Douay translators, working from that Latin, kept its word: charity.

Caritas comes from carus: dear, precious. Charity once meant holding someone dear because they're precious. Over time, English shrank it down to donations; the old translation lets you hear the big meaning again.
Third, the Catechism. Paragraph 221 says John's line reaches all the way down: love isn't just something God does, or feels now and then.
God's very being is love. Tomorrow, why Catholics say that love has a shape. For today: in Catholic teaching, the God who told Moses I AM is love all the way through.
Paul describes charity in his first letter to the Corinthians: "Charity is patient, is kind: charity envieth not." It's often read at weddings.
Paul's word there is agape too, so read beside John, it becomes a portrait of God. That's why John can say the one who doesn't love doesn't know God.
For Catholics, God is known less by argument than by love, given and received. In 2005, Pope Benedict XVI chose those three Latin words as the title of his first encyclical.

how: Catholics count charity, love of God and neighbor, as the greatest of the three theological virtues, and practice it through the corporal and spiritual works of mercy.

o: a gift of money to people in need

games.q: God is charity — tap the pairs.

s: in the Douay-Rheims, charity means giving money
it translates agape and caritas: love that holds someone dear.
the Catechism says God's very being is love
CCC 221: love isn't just something God does.
Paul's 'charity is patient, is kind' uses the same Greek word as John's 'God is charity'
both are agape. it's read at weddings, but beside John it reads as a portrait of God.

games.q: you've done something kind for someone. what does Jesus say to do with the credit?
o: post about it to inspire others
let not your left hand know what your right hand does
games.why: in Matthew 6, Jesus says to give in secret. charity in the old sense doesn't need an audience.

practice: Think of someone near you, at home, at work, down the street, and one small loving thing you could do for them that no one will notice: refill something, fix something, pray for them, leave a kind word.
Picture yourself doing it quietly, with no credit; Jesus said to give so that your left hand doesn't know what your right hand is doing. If you pray, you can offer it ahead of time.

wordCard.voice: Agape, the Greek word behind 'God is charity': the love that gives itself away for another's good, which Catholics say is God's very being. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: love that gives itself for another's good, the word John uses in God is love.

carryVoice: Your line: god is love. That's charity in the old, big sense. See you tomorrow.
